newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian central bank says credit environment poor.
newsitem.headline: Latvian central bank says credit environment poor.

text.p: Latvian central bank governor Einars Repse said on Wednesday that the country's infant banking sector still lacked a proper legal environment for extending credit resources.
"There is an overflow of commercial credit resources in Latvia," Repse told a news conference.
"But the total volume of loans to businesses and individuals has remained the same at 220 million lats over the past four months," he said.
Repse noted that deposits have grown by by 14 percent since December 1995 to 357 million lats in October this year.
But he said that banks prefered investing in foreign securities or Latvian Treasury bills to lending locally.
"Demand for T-bills always exceeds the supply...this signifies no lack of credit in the system," he said.

"Banks are afraid, and understandably so, to give loans because of the risks involved - lack of collateral and a free land market, no proper legal framework, and the lack of a reliable and transparent history about the performance of enterprises," he added.
"We should not drag our feet (in resolving these issues)," he said, and urged parliament to work quickly to create a favourable legal environment for the extension of credit.

Latvia, which quit the former Soviet Union five years ago, is still recovering from the affects of a crisis that rocked its banking sector last year with the surprise closure of its largest bank, Banka Baltija.
The country has 33 licensed banks but only 12 are allowed to accept deposits from individuals.

Analysts predict a wave of mergers in the sector but Repse said that most of the country's banks would probably stand on their own until 1998, when the minumum capital requirement will rise to two million lats from one million.
